items.stem:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

The Return of the Millets

1. For most of the twentieth century, rice and wheat dominated Indian plates. Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi, once the staple food of many regions, came to be seen as "poor people's grain". Farmers switched to crops that the market rewarded, and a generation grew up without ever tasting a ragi roti.

2. Today millets are making a comeback. Nutritionists point out that they are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and that they release sugar into the blood slowly, which helps people with diabetes. Urban shops now sell millet biscuits, noodles and breakfast cereals, often at prices higher than those of rice.

3. Millets are also kind to the land. They grow on dry, poor soil and need far less water than rice. In a country where groundwater levels are falling, a crop that can survive on rain alone is a valuable insurance against drought. Many millets are also ready for harvest in a short season.

4. The year 2023 was declared the International Year of Millets by the United Nations, on a proposal made by India. Schools have added millet dishes to their midday meals, and food festivals celebrate traditional recipes that grandmothers never forgot.

5. The challenge now is to make sure that farmers, and not only food companies, benefit from the revival. Fair prices, good seeds and storage facilities will decide whether millets return to fields or remain an expensive trend in city supermarkets.

(i) Why did millets come to be seen as "poor people's grain"?
(ii) What happened to a generation of Indians, according to paragraph 1?  (a) They stopped eating wheat  (b) They grew up without tasting a ragi roti  (c) They became farmers  (d) They ate only millets
(iii) Why are millets good for people with diabetes?  (a) They are expensive  (b) They contain no fibre  (c) They are sweet  (d) They release sugar into the blood slowly
(iv) Name two nutrients found in millets, according to the passage.
(v) Why are millets described as "kind to the land"?
(vi) A crop that survives on rain alone is called "insurance against drought" because …  (a) it is insured by the government  (b) it is costly  (c) it grows only in floods  (d) it can still be harvested when water is scarce
(vii) Which year was the International Year of Millets?  (a) 2023  (b) 2030  (c) 2013  (d) 2020
(viii) What is the main challenge mentioned in the last paragraph?
(ix) The writer fears millets may remain …  (a) an expensive trend in city supermarkets  (b) banned  (c) unknown in cities  (d) only an export
(x) The tone of the last paragraph is …  (a) bitterly angry  (b) cautiously hopeful  (c) completely indifferent  (d) humorous
items.answer: (i) Rice and wheat dominated and the market rewarded them, so millets were looked down upon. (ii) (b) They grew up without tasting a ragi roti (iii) (d) They release sugar into the blood slowly (iv) Any two of fibre, iron and calcium. (v) They grow on dry, poor soil and need much less water than rice. (vi) (d) it can still be harvested when water is scarce (vii) (a) 2023 (viii) Making sure farmers benefit, through fair prices, good seeds and storage. (ix) (a) an expensive trend in city supermarkets (x) (b) cautiously hopeful

(ii) (b) They grew up without tasting a ragi roti (iii) (d) They release sugar into the blood slowly (iv) Any two of fibre, iron and calcium. (v) They grow on dry, poor soil and need much less water than rice. (vi) (d) it can still be harvested when water is scarce (vii) (a) 2023 (viii) Making sure farmers benefit, through fair prices, good seeds and storage. (ix) (a) an expensive trend in city supermarkets (x) (b) cautiously hopeful (1 mark each, 10 marks.)

Read the survey report and answer the questions that follow.

A survey on care for elderly neighbours was carried out in Chandigarh in 2025. 800 residents of a housing society were asked how often they spend time with elderly people in their area. The results were: daily – 39%; every week – 6%; once a month – 32%; hardly ever – 23%. The word "companionship" came up often in the discussion that followed the survey.

(i) Which response was the most common?  (a) every week  (b) hardly ever  (c) daily  (d) once a month
(ii) Which response was the least common?  (a) hardly ever  (b) once a month  (c) daily  (d) every week
(iii) How many residents of a housing society chose "daily"?  (a) 3120  (b) 312  (c) 39  (d) 184
(iv) Did more than half of the residents of a housing society choose "daily"? Give the figure.

(d) The survey was carried out in Patna.
(vi) In the passage, the word "companionship" means …  (a) the pleasure of being with others  (b) communication by letters or messages  (c) calming  (d) the amount used
(vii) Write one suggestion the organisers could make, based on the survey on care for elderly neighbours.

Read the passage given below and make notes on it in points only, using headings and sub-headings and at least four recognisable abbreviations. Supply a suitable title.

Reading aloud is often thought of as something only parents do for small children, but its benefits continue at every age. When children hear stories read aloud, they learn new words, the rhythm of sentences and the pleasure of a good plot long before they can read such books themselves. For teenagers, reading aloud improves pronunciation, confidence and the ability to speak in public. Teachers find that a class that reads a play aloud understands the characters better than one that reads silently. Reading aloud also brings people together: grandparents who read to grandchildren build strong bonds, and reading groups for the elderly reduce loneliness. Doctors note that reading aloud slows our breathing and can calm anxiety. To make it effective, one should choose texts that suit the listeners, vary the voice for different characters and pause to talk about what has been read.

Social and health benefits: (a) bonds b/w grandparents and grandchildren (b) less loneliness among elderly (c) slower breathing, less anxiety. 4. Tips: (a) suitable texts (b) vary voice (c) pause and discuss. Key: vocab. – vocabulary; b/w – between.

items.stem:
Read the passage given below and write a summary of it in about 50 words. Give it a suitable title.

Trees are often the first casualty when a city grows, yet they are among its most useful residents. A large tree can lower the temperature of the street beneath it by several degrees, reducing the need for air-conditioning in nearby buildings. Its leaves trap dust and absorb harmful gases, so roads lined with trees have cleaner air. Roots hold the soil and help rainwater soak into the ground instead of flooding streets. Trees also give shelter to birds, squirrels and insects, bringing a little wildness into concrete neighbourhoods. Studies show that people who can see trees from their windows feel less stressed, and patients in hospitals with green views recover sooner. Cities can protect trees by planning roads around old ones, choosing native species for new planting and involving residents in caring for saplings. A tree planted today is a gift to people not yet born.
items.answer: City trees cool streets, clean the air, prevent flooding, shelter wildlife and improve people's health and mood. Cities should protect old trees, plant native species and involve residents in caring for them.
items.markingKey: Content 2 (all key points, in one's own words), expression 1 (coherent, within the word limit). Model summary: City trees cool streets, clean the air, prevent flooding, shelter wildlife and improve people's health and mood. Cities should protect old trees, plant native species and involve residents in caring for them.

Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

The Library That Travels

1. Every Saturday morning, a blue van painted with storybook characters stops at the edge of a small settlement outside the city. Within minutes, children come running, some still in their slippers, to choose a book for the week.

2. The mobile library was started by a group of retired teachers who noticed that the nearest public library was more than ten kilometres away. With donated books and a second-hand van, they began with fifty books. Today they carry over two thousand in Hindi, English and two regional languages.

3. The volunteers do more than lend books. They read aloud to the youngest children, help older ones with difficult words and hold small quizzes. A few mothers who never went to school have started borrowing picture books to learn to read with their children.

4. The project faces problems. Books get lost or damaged in the rains, fuel costs rise every year and volunteers are getting older. Yet the organisers say that every returned book with a dog-eared page is proof that it has been read.

5. Their dream is to train young people from the settlement itself to run the van one day, so that the library belongs to the community it serves.

(i) When does the library van visit the settlement?  (a) On holidays only  (b) Once a month  (c) Every evening  (d) Every Saturday morning
(ii) What does "some still in their slippers" suggest about the children?
(iii) Who started the mobile library?  (a) Schoolchildren  (b) A group of retired teachers  (c) The city government  (d) A publishing company
(iv) How many books do they carry now?  (a) Fifty  (b) Ten thousand  (c) Five hundred  (d) Over two thousand

(ix) What is the organisers' dream?
(x) The library will "belong to the community" when …  (a) it closes  (b) teachers own it  (c) local young people run it  (d) it is sold

Read the passage given below and make notes on it in points only, using headings and sub-headings and at least four recognisable abbreviations. Supply a suitable title.

Every year millions of tonnes of plastic find their way into the oceans. Much of it comes from rivers that carry waste from cities, and from fishing nets that are lost or thrown away at sea. Once in the water, plastic does not disappear; sunlight and waves break it into tiny pieces called microplastics. Sea turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, seabirds feed bottle caps to their chicks, and fish swallow microplastics that later reach our dinner plates. The problem can be reduced. Governments can ban single-use plastics and improve waste collection. Companies can design packaging that is reusable or easy to recycle. Each of us can carry cloth bags, refuse plastic straws and join beach clean-ups. Scientists are also testing enzymes and bacteria that can break plastic down. The ocean has no voice of its own, but our everyday choices can speak for it.

Solutions: 3.1 govt.: ban single-use plastics, better waste collection; 3.2 cos.: reusable/recyclable packaging; 3.3 individuals: cloth bags, no straws, beach clean-ups; 3.4 scientists: enzymes, bacteria. Key: govt. – government; cos. – companies.

items.stem:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

The Library That Travels

1. Every Saturday morning, a blue van painted with storybook characters stops at the edge of a small settlement outside the city. Within minutes, children come running, some still in their slippers, to choose a book for the week.

2. The mobile library was started by a group of retired teachers who noticed that the nearest public library was more than ten kilometres away. With donated books and a second-hand van, they began with fifty books. Today they carry over two thousand in Hindi, English and two regional languages.

3. The volunteers do more than lend books. They read aloud to the youngest children, help older ones with difficult words and hold small quizzes. A few mothers who never went to school have started borrowing picture books to learn to read with their children.

4. The project faces problems. Books get lost or damaged in the rains, fuel costs rise every year and volunteers are getting older. Yet the organisers say that every returned book with a dog-eared page is proof that it has been read.

5. Their dream is to train young people from the settlement itself to run the van one day, so that the library belongs to the community it serves.

(i) What does "some still in their slippers" suggest about the children?
(ii) Who started the mobile library?  (a) A group of retired teachers  (b) Schoolchildren  (c) The city government  (d) A publishing company
(iii) Why was the mobile library needed?
(iv) How many books do they carry now?  (a) Five hundred  (b) Over two thousand  (c) Ten thousand  (d) Fifty
(v) Which word in paragraph 2 means "given free as a gift"?  (a) retired  (b) carried  (c) noticed  (d) donated
(vi) Name two things the volunteers do besides lending books.
(vii) Who have started borrowing picture books?  (a) Retired teachers  (b) Shopkeepers  (c) Mothers who never went to school  (d) Drivers
(viii) Name two problems the project faces.
(ix) For the organisers, a dog-eared page is proof that …  (a) the book has been read  (b) the book is new  (c) the reader is careless  (d) the van is old
(x) The library will "belong to the community" when …  (a) local young people run it  (b) it is sold  (c) teachers own it  (d) it closes
items.answer: (i) They are so eager that they rush out without getting ready. (ii) (a) A group of retired teachers (iii) The nearest public library was more than ten kilometres away. (iv) (b) Over two thousand (v) (d) donated (vi) Read aloud, help with difficult words, hold quizzes (any two). (vii) (c) Mothers who never went to school (viii) Books lost or damaged in rain, rising fuel costs, ageing volunteers (any two). (ix) (a) the book has been read (x) (a) local young people run it
items.markingKey: (i) They are so eager that they rush out without getting ready. (ii) (a) A group of retired teachers (iii) The nearest public library was more than ten kilometres away. (iv) (b) Over two thousand (v) (d) donated (vi) Read aloud, help with difficult words, hold quizzes (any two). (vii) (c) Mothers who never went to school (viii) Books lost or damaged in rain, rising fuel costs, ageing volunteers (any two). Read the survey report and answer the questions that follow.

A survey on water use was carried out in Varanasi in 2025. 400 families were asked which activity uses most of their daily water. The results were: bathing – 8%; washing clothes – 21%; cooking and drinking – 9%; cleaning the house – 27%; gardening – 35%. The organisers said the findings would help them plan better, and they encouraged people to think about how they conserve and use their time and resources.

(i) Which response was the least common?  (a) gardening  (b) washing clothes  (c) cleaning the house  (d) bathing
(ii) How many families chose "bathing"?  (a) 32  (b) 8  (c) 140  (d) 320
(iii) What percentage of families chose one of the two most common responses taken together?  (a) 62%  (b) 38%  (c) 35%  (d) 72%
(iv) Did more than half of the families choose "gardening"? Give the figure.

(viii) Any practical suggestion that follows from the figures – 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the passage given below and make notes on it in points only, using headings and sub-headings and at least four recognisable abbreviations. Supply a suitable title.

As examinations approach, many students feel anxious, sleep badly and lose their appetite. A little stress can sharpen attention, but too much makes it hard to remember what one has studied. Counsellors suggest a few simple steps. First, make a realistic timetable that divides the syllabus into small parts and leaves time for revision. Second, take short breaks every hour; a walk or a few stretches refresh the mind. Third, sleep for at least seven hours, because the brain stores what we have learnt while we sleep. Fourth, eat regular meals and drink enough water instead of living on snacks and tea. Finally, talk to someone – a parent, friend or teacher – when worry becomes overwhelming. Comparing oneself with others usually adds to the pressure; it is more useful to compare today's preparation with yesterday's.
items.answer: Title: Coping with Exam Stress. 1. Effects of stress: (a) anxiety (b) poor sleep (c) loss of appetite (d) too much stress affects memory. 2. Counsellors' tips: (a) realistic timetable – small parts, revision time (b) short breaks every hr. (c) min. 7 hrs sleep (d) regular meals, enough water (e) talk to parent/friend/teacher. 3. Attitude: compare with own past, not with others. Key: hr. – hour; min. – minimum; hrs – hours.
items.markingKey: Title 1; abbreviations with key 1; content in a proper note format (headings, sub-headings, indentation) 3. Model notes: Title: Coping with Exam Stress. 1. Counsellors suggest a few simple steps. First, make a realistic timetable that divides the syllabus into small parts and leaves time for revision.
